                          we are providing this early version of the manuscript. The manuscript will undergo copyediting, typesetting, and review of the resulting
                          proof before it is published in its final citable form. Please note that during the production process errors may be discovered which could
                          affect the content, and all legal disclaimers that apply to the journal pertain.
                           Edelman et al.                                                                     Page 2

NIH-PA Author Manuscript  1. Introduction

NIH-PA Author Manuscript                    Forty-nine percent of all pregnancies in the United States are unintended, and about half of
                                            these occur in couples using contraception [1]. Recent epidemiologic evidence suggests that
                                            obese women may have higher rates of hormonal contraceptive failure than women of normal
                                            body mass indices (BMI) [2,3]. However, this finding is not present in many studies [4-6]. If
                                            a difference in contraceptive efficacy does exist, identifying the mechanism for failure is critical
                                            to creating a contraceptive strategy with better efficacy for obese women.

                                            In general, the effect of obesity on drug pharmacokinetics is poorly understood. This is
                                            particularly true of oral contraceptives (OCs), as most investigational studies have excluded
                                            women over 130% of ideal body weight, and no prior studies exist regarding OC
                                            pharmacokinetics in obese women. Depending on the drug studied, BMI can affect
                                            pharmacokinetics in several different ways including bioavailability and hepatic clearance
                                            [alterations in enzymatic proteins (CYP3A activity)], renal clearance (alterations in glomerular
                                            filtration and/or secretion), and volume of distribution (lipophilic properties and/or alterations
                                            in levels of drug binding proteins) [7].

                                            The main contraceptive effect of OCs is via negative feedback inhibition of the hypothalamic-
                                            pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis, which has only been studied in normal BMI women [8]. A
                                            difference in OC pharmacokinetics due to obesity could lead to inadequate suppression of the
                                            HPO axis, thus allowing follicular development to occur leading to ovulation. This study was
                                            designed to determine whether increased BMI affects OC pharmacokinetics and the
                                            suppression of the HPO axis.

NIH-PA Author Manuscript  2. Materials and methods

                                            A prospective cohort study was conducted at Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU) in
                                            Portland, Oregon, from March 2006 to September 2007. The OHSU Institutional Review Board
                                            and OHSU Clinical & Translational Research Institute (OCTRI) approved the study protocol
                                            and all patients underwent informed written consent.

                                            Twenty, healthy, reproductive-aged (18-35 years old) women, not currently using hormonal
                                            contraception but seeking to initiate contraception with COCs, were recruited. Subjects were
                                            either of normal (BMI < 25 kg/m2) or obese BMI (BMI >30 kg/m2) with regular menstrual
                                            cycles, not actively seeking weight gain or loss, no evidence of anemia (hematocrit  36%),
                                            no contraindications to hormonal contraception, no use of tobacco or drugs known to interfere
                                            with the metabolism of sex steroids, and no overt clinical features of or prior treatment for
                                            metabolic disorders (i.e., polycystic ovarian syndrome).

                                            To ensure enrollment of ovulatory women, a progesterone level of 3 ng/mL was confirmed
                                            during the luteal phase (Days 18 to 25) of the menstrual cycle prior to treatment with OCs.
                                            Demographic information was gathered along with several obesity biomarkers including
                                            weight, height, body composition measurements by air displacement plethysmorgraphy, and
                                            waist-to-hip ratios.

                                            All study subjects were placed on a combination monophasic birth control pill containing 20
                                            mcg ethinyl estradiol (EE)/100 mcg levonorgestrel (LNG) (Alesse; Wyeth, Madison, NJ) at

                                            fashion (21 days active pill with a 7-day hormone-free interval) for a total of two treatment
                                            cycles. Women were instructed to take the pill at 0900 AM daily. Self-reported compliance
                                            with the medication was recorded on a calendar and women were also asked to contact
                                            investigators if there was a delay in time of pill ingestion and/or missed 2 or more pills in 1

                                          The study flow is illustrated in Fig. 1. Serum samples were obtained during two 48-h inpatient

NIH-PA Author Manuscript  2.1. Pharmacokinetics & Sex Hormone Binding Globulin: timing of samples and assay
                          characteristics
NIH-PA Author Manuscript
                                            As pharmacokinetic measurements can vary after single and multiple dose exposure, samples
                                            were obtained at two specific time points that represent the cumulative steady-state exposure
                                            of a 21-day cycle [following 21 days of active pills (Cycle 1, Day 21-Day 22)] and the effect
                                            of re-initiation of the next cycle after the 7-day hormone-free interval (Cycle 1, Day 28-Cycle
                                            2, Day 1) (see Fig. 1). EE and LNG levels were measured in serum samples collected during
                                            the first inpatient stay on Cycle 1, Day 21 at 0 (0900 AM; time of drug ingestion), and 0.5, 1,
                                            1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 h and continued on Cycle 1, Day 22 (first day of hormone-free interval in
                                            Cycle 1 at 0 (0900 AM), 4, 8, 12, 24 h. This process was repeated on Cycle 1, Day 28 (last day
                                            of the hormone-free interval) until the completion of the second 48-h stay except the sampling
                                            protocol was reversed [starting on Cycle 1, Day 28 at 0, 4, 8, 12 h and then initiating the more
                                            intensive monitoring at time zero (0900 AM) on Cycle 2, Day 1 (first active treatment day of
                                            Cycle 2)].

                                            Assays were performed at the University of Southern California. LNG and EE levels in serum
                                            samples were quantified by specific and sensitive radioimmunoassays (RIAs) as described
                                            previously [9,10]. Prior to RIA, each analyte was extracted with ethyl acetate:hexane (3:2) and
                                            separated by Celite column partition chromatography to remove interfering steroids.
                                            Procedural losses were estimated by adding approximately 800 dpm of titrated internal standard
                                            (3H-LNG or 3H-EE) to the serum prior to the extraction step. The losses ranged from 20-30%
                                            and the values were used to correct the RIA results. A highly specific antiserum was used in
                                            conjunction with an iodinated radioligand in each RIA. Separation of free from antiserum-
                                            bound LNG or EE was achieved by use of a second antibody. The sensitivities of these RIAs
                                            are 0.05 ng/mL for LNG and 15 pg/mL for EE. Intra-assay and inter-assay coefficients of
                                            variation are 4.4% and 8.9% for LNG RIAs and 6.9% and 11% for EE RIAs, respectively.

                                            Additionally, since sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) binds LNG and could potentially
                                            lower the amount of free LNG, SHBG levels were assayed in serum on Cycle 1, Day 21 and
                                            Cycle 1, Day 28. SHBG was quantified by a solid-phase, two-site chemiluminescent
                                            immunoassay using the Immulite Analyzer (Siemens Medical Solutions Diagnostics, Los
                                            Angeles, CA). The solid phase is a polystyrene bead with a monoclonal antibody specific for
                                            SHBG. The intra-assay CVs range from 4.1% to 7.7% and the inter-assay CVs range from
                                            5.8% to 11%.

                                            1) and Cycle 2, Day 1 (first active treatment day of Cycle 2). In addition, blood samples were
                                            drawn at 0 (0900 AM), 4, and 8 h daily during both 48-h stays and then twice per week during
                                            Cycle 2 for steroid hormone [estradiol (E2) and progesterone (P)] analyses.

                                          1, Day 21 (baseline) and then collected at time intervals most likely to capture follicular activity
                                          [Day 28 and once during the first week of Cycle 2 (Day 5,6, or 7)]. Inhibin B was measured
                                          by ELISA using an enzymatically amplified two-site, two-step, sandwich-type ELISA
                                          (Diagnostic Systems Laboratories, Webster, TX). The intra-assay CVs range from 3.5% to
                                          5.6%, and the interassay CVs range from 6.2% to 7.6%.

NIH-PA Author Manuscript  2.3. Pharmacokinetic and pulsatile parameter analysis

                                            2.3.1. Pharmacokinetics--LNG and EE pharmacokinetic data from the first and second
                                            inpatient stays were analyzed separately by noncompartmental methods using WinNonLin
                                            (Pharsight, Mountain View, CA; v 5.2). Maximum serum LNG and EE concentrations
                                            (Cmax) and time to maximum concentration (Tmax) were observed values. Area under the curve
                                            (AUC) was calculated from time zero to 48 h (AUC0-t) using the linear trapezoidal rule and
                                            then extrapolated to infinity (AUC0-) which provides a more accurate calculation of drug
                                            clearance [11]. Drug half-life (t1/2), oral clearance (CL), and volume of distribution (VD) were
                                            generated using standard pharmacokinetic calculations (t1/2= 0.693/z, where z is the terminal
                                            elimination rate constant; CL= dose/AUC0-; VD= CL//z). One normal BMI subject exhibited
                                            out of range values for clearance; thus, she was excluded from the pharmacokinetic analyses.

NIH-PA Author Manuscript                  2.3.2. LH pulsatility--The deconvolution method was used to analyze the pulsatile
                                          characteristics of each LH series using analytic software provided by the University of
                                          Virginia's Center for Biological Timing (weblink:
                                          http://mljohnson.pharm.virginia.edu/home.html) [12]. This estimation algorithm resulted in
                                          estimates of the number of LH pulses, half-life (t1/2), average pulse mass, total hormone
                                          secreted, and inter-pulse interval. Missing data were minimal with the exception of one obese
                                          subject who was missing 8 points (2 h) at the start of the second day of observation (Cycle 2,
                                          Day 1) due to a nonfunctional I.V. site. This subjects' series was truncated for analysis and the
                                          number of pulses extrapolated to the 8-h time period of observation. All other missing data
                                          points were linearly interpolated prior to the deconvolution analysis.

                                            Differences between normal and obese BMI group demographic and obesity biomarker
                                            measures (weight, height, body composition measurements by air displacement
                                            plethysmorgraphy, and waist-to-hip ratios) were assessed using a two-sample t-test (or chi-
                                            squared for race/ethnicity). In addition, inhibin levels were compared between BMI groups
                                            using a two-sample t-test and SHGB levels were compared between BMI groups using a two-
                                            sample t-test and between days using a paired t-test. Repeated measures analysis of variance
                                            (RMANOVA) was used to assess whether changes between Cycle 1, Day 28 and Cycle 2, Day
                                            1 differed between the obese and normal BMI groups on any of the pharmacokinetic or pulsatile
                                            parameters. To further understand differences, pair-wise comparisons were performed between
                                            groups on Cycle 1, Day 28 and Cycle 1, Day 2 using a two-sample t-test and within groups

NIH-PA Author Manuscript  3. Results

NIH-PA Author Manuscript                    Thirty-six subjects were screened for the study with 20 subjects (10 obese, 10 normal BMI)
                                            meeting eligibility criteria and completing the study (1 subject lost to follow-up prior to luteal
                                            phase P, 9 subjects with luteal phase P < 3 ng/mL, 1 subject with uncontrolled hypertension,
                                            1 subject pregnant, 1 subject discontinued secondary to undesired OC side effects, 1 subject
                                            withdrawn from study due to OC noncompliance, 2 subjects unable to complete inpatient
                                            visits).

                          3.1. Demographics

                                            There were no significant demographic differences between groups except mean BMI, waist/
                                            hip ratio, and percent body fat were significantly greater (p < 0.05) in the obese compared to
                                            the normal BMI group (see Table 1).

                          3.2. Pharmacokinetics

                                            Fig. 2 and 3 depict the LNG and EE pharmacokinetic parameters. The top two panels of each
                                            figure display serum concentration versus time curves at two different time intervals; the end
                                            of Cycle 1 (after 21 days of active hormone use but before the hormone-free interval) and at
                                            the beginning of Cycle 2 (after a 7-day hormone-free interval and re-initiating active hormone
                                            use). The box plots below in Fig. 2 and 3 represent each of the individual pharmacokinetic
                                            parameter values (i.e., T1/2, Tmax, Cmax, AUC, Vd, and CL) for both BMI groups at the two
                                            time points studied.

                                            The Cmax, Tmax, and AUC were directly derived for the serum concentration versus time curves
                                            (Fig. 2 and 3). No differences were found in mean Cmax and mean Tmax for LNG or EE between
                                            BMI groups at either time point. However, a significant difference in mean AUC for both EE
                                            and LNG existed between BMI groups at the end of Cycle 1 (after 21 days of active hormonal
                                            exposure) with a larger AUC in the obese group as compared to the normal BMI group (p <
                                            0.05).

                                            With a larger mean AUC, mean T1/2 was significantly longer (LNG p < 0.05) and CL was
                                            significantly less in the obese group (LNG and EE p < 0.05). This also correlates with a lower
                                            but not statistically significant maximum LNG concentration on Cycle 2, Day 1 [1.9 ng/mL
                                            (SD 0.5) versus 2.5 ng/mL (SD 0.7)]. There were no differences in volume of distribution
                                            (Vd) for either EE or LNG between groups at either time point.

                                            SHBG levels were no different between groups, but significantly different between days (p <
                                            0.05) with lower levels found following the 7-day hormone-free interval [mean 49 nmol/L (SD
                                            16)] and higher levels following 21 days of OC use [mean 70 nmol/L (SD 23)].

                                            [average number of pulses: normal BMI 5 (SD 2), obese BMI 6 (SD 1); average inter-pulse
                                            interval: normal BMI 102 min (SD 54), obese BMI 82 (SD 26)]. Fig. 4 depicts the gonadotropin

NIH-PA Author Manuscript  4. Discussion

                                            While some (but not all) epidemiologic studies suggest that obesity reduces the efficacy of
                                            OCs, a mechanism for this effect has not been elucidated [2,3]. The current study was designed
                                            to determine whether obesity alters the pharmacokinetics of OCs and results in inadequate
                                            HPO axis suppression and ovulation. Our results show significant differences in LNG half-
                                            life, clearance and time to reach steady-state between obese and normal BMI women.
                                            Consistent with these changes, more obese women demonstrated hormonal changes associated
                                            with recruitment and maturation of a dominant follicle, and even ovulation but the sample size
                                            was too small to achieve statistical significance.

                                            It is widely assumed that hormonal contraceptive failure in obese subjects is due to lower
                                            plasma concentrations of contraceptive steroid hormones arising out of greater drug
                                            distribution in the fat mass. Unexpectedly, our results demonstrated no differences in LNG or
                                            EE volume of distribution between obese and normal BMI subjects. Instead, we found that
                                            obesity adversely affected the time to reach LNG steady-state due to a larger mean AUC. The
                                            LNG half-life (T1/2) in obese subjects was twice that of normal BMI subjects, and therefore
                                            the time to reach steady state (approximately 5-7 * T1/2) was doubled (obese BMI 10 days
                                            versus normal BMI 5 days; p < 0.05; Fig 6). This prolonged time suggests that obese women
                                            using OCs may require a longer time interval following resumption of active pills to experience
                                            inhibitory drug concentrations, and that this creates a "window of opportunity" for follicular
                                            recruitment, ovulation, and even pregnancy. The length of this "window" may vary
                                            significantly, as one obese subject (BMI = 37) had a calculated time to reach steady-state of
                                            greater than 20 days and may have never been adequately suppressed for the entire OC cycle.

NIH-PA Author Manuscript                  Little is known regarding drug pharmacokinetics in the obese population. Obesity reportedly
                                          decreases CYP3A activity in animal studies [13,14]. However, data in humans are conflicting
NIH-PA Author Manuscript                  [14]. Since the major route of EE metabolism is through the cytochrome p450 enzyme system,
                                          we expected and found a decrease in the total clearance of EE in obese subjects. Also, EE
NIH-PA Author Manuscript                  clearance values in both BMI groups increased from the beginning to end of the hormone-free
                                          interval. In other words, the 7-day hormone-free or EE exposure-free interval normalized EE
                                          clearance.

                                          With EE inhibiting the cytochrome p450 enzyme system in the liver and increasing binding
                                          proteins (SHBG) during chronic EE exposure, we expected and found a decrease in the total
                                          clearance of LNG and an increase in LNG volume of distribution in both BMI groups from the
                                          beginning versus the end of the hormone-free interval [15,16,17,19]. However, the obese group
                                          had a significantly lower clearance than the normal BMI group at the beginning of the hormone-
                                          free interval even with similar levels of binding proteins (SHBG). This suggests that 21 days
                                          of EE exposure affects the metabolism/clearance of LNG via unidentified metabolic pathways.

                                          The corresponding gonadotropin and ovarian hormone data support conclusions from the
                                          pharmacokinetic observations that differences exist between OC users of differing BMI.
                                          Evidence of HPO reactivation was present in both groups, however the number of pulses and
                                          inter-pulse interval at the end of the hormone-free interval in the obese BMI group were more
                                          consistent with follicular phase activity [8]. Although not statistically significant,
                                          physiologically, even small differences in gonadotropin levels, like we found, are important
                                          with only a 10% rise in FSH triggering follicle growth and a difference in 1 pulse indicating
                                          follicular rather than luteal phase activity [8]. Consistent with follicular development, mean
                                          FSH levels were lower in the obese group as E2 levels began to rise. In addition, more obese
                                          than normal BMI women demonstrated E2 and P levels consistent with follicular development
                                          and ovulation during the first 7-10 days of Cycle 2. Overall, the differences observed are of
                                          potential clinical significance.

                                          Collectively, these data provide evidence that biologic differences exist between OC users of
                                          differing BMIs and that this may affect OC efficacy. However, there are several limitations to
                                          this study. By limiting the BMI categories to normal and obese (excluding the overweight
                                          category), we hoped to maximize the possible effect of size in this study. Several epidemiologic
                                          studies have shown that even women in the overweight BMI (25-30 kg/m2) category may be
                                          at increased risk for contraceptive failure [2,3]. Perhaps the risk of failure increases linearly as
                                          BMI increases, although a sub-analysis of several of our heaviest subjects (BMI  40 kg/m2)
                                          revealed no pharmacokinetic differences from the other obese subjects. In addition, the choice
                                          of an OC with the lowest EE component (20 mcg) was deliberately made to maximize the
                                          ability to detect a mechanism of action for OC failure; this choice also correlated well with
                                          current clinical practice. Although no differences in thrombosis risk have been found between
                                          an OC with a 20 mcg versus 30 mcg EE component, it has been observed that many clinicians
                                          preferentially prescribe these very-low estrogen dose pills to obese women in an effort to
                                          decrease their risk of venous thrombosis. Additionally, our pharmacokinetic data were found
                                          to have wide intra-subject variability. Intra-subject variability is due to inherent variations
                                          among subjects and within analytic assays. However, the variability of our EE and LNG
                                          analytical assays was low (10%) and our intrasubject variability (30-60%) was consistent with
                                          findings of published studies [19]. Our sampling length of 8 h at 15 min intervals only
                                          performed at the end of the 7-day hormone-free interval may have impaired our ability to
                                          determine a statistical difference in LH pulse parameters between groups although this is the
                                          first report on gonadotropin pulsatility in obese OC users. As prior studies have shown some
                                          escape of the HPO axis from OC inhibition at the end of the 7-day hormone-free interval in
                                          normal BMI women, we chose this time point to monitor for HPO axis escape in obese women

NIH-PA Author Manuscript                  [20,21]. Finally, our study provides only indirect measures of follicle development and
                                          ovulation and does not address all potential contraceptive mechanisms or fertility.

                                          Although this study gives credence to the hypothesis that BMI affects OC pharmacokinetics
                                          resulting in greater follicle development and possible ovulation, essential factors in OC
                                          efficacy, additional studies are needed before we recommend a change in clinical practice in
                                          regard to use of oral contraception in obese women.

"""Write the combined pill's SHBG curves into app/pill_comparison.html.

With SHBG the model has no simple formula, so the page can't recompute it in the
browser. This script runs the Python model and replaces the data block between
the /*DATA*/ and /*END DATA*/ markers in the page.

Usage:  python scripts/export_comparison_data.py
"""

import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT / "src"))

from minipill.params import LEVONORGESTREL, LEVONORGESTREL_DOSE_MG, SHBG  # noqa: E402
from minipill.pk import mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml, simulate  # noqa: E402

DAY = 24.0
PAGE = ROOT / "app" / "pill_comparison.html"
PACK = [d * DAY for d in range(21)]
DUE = 14 * DAY  # the day-15 pill
MONTH_STEP, LATE_STEP = 0.2, 0.25  # hours
LATE_WINDOW = (-24.0, 96.0)  # hours around DUE
LATE_OPTIONS = [x / 2 for x in range(48)] + ["skip", "skip2"]  # 0, 0.5, ... 23.5 h late


def run(doses, t):
    sim = simulate(LEVONORGESTREL, sorted(doses), LEVONORGESTREL_DOSE_MG, t, shbg=SHBG)
    return mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(sim.conc), sim.shbg


def scenario(late):
    if late == "skip":
        return [d for d in PACK if d != DUE]
    if late == "skip2":  # CDC: pills 15 and 16 missed; missed pill + pill 17 taken together at +48 h
        return [d for d in PACK if d not in (DUE, DUE + DAY)] + [DUE + 2 * DAY]
    return [d for d in PACK if d != DUE] + [DUE + late]


def main():
    t_month = np.arange(0, 28 * DAY + 1e-9, MONTH_STEP)
    c_month, s_month = run(PACK, t_month)

    t_late = np.arange(0, DUE + LATE_WINDOW[1] + 1e-9, LATE_STEP)
    c_on, _ = run(PACK, t_late)
    low = c_on[int(round(DUE / LATE_STEP))]
    first = int(round((DUE + LATE_WINDOW[0]) / LATE_STEP))
    late = {}
    for opt in LATE_OPTIONS:
        c, _ = run(scenario(opt), t_late)
        late[opt if isinstance(opt, str) else f"{opt:g}"] = [round(100 * v / low, 1) for v in c[first:]]

    data = {
        "monthStep": MONTH_STEP,
        "month": [round(float(v), 4) for v in c_month],
        "shbg": [round(float(v), 2) for v in s_month],
        "lateStep": LATE_STEP,
        "lateStart": LATE_WINDOW[0],
        "usualLow": round(float(low), 4),
        "late": late,
    }
    block = "/*DATA*/ const LNG_SHBG = " + json.dumps(data, separators=(",", ":")) + "; /*END DATA*/"
    html = PAGE.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    new, n = re.subn(r"/\*DATA\*/.*?/\*END DATA\*/", lambda _: block, html, flags=re.S)
    if n != 1:
        raise SystemExit("data markers not found in page")
    PAGE.write_text(new, encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"Wrote {len(block) / 1024:.0f} KB of data; usual low {low:.3f} ng/mL")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

1	"""Write the combined pill's SHBG curves into app/pill_comparison.html.
2	
3	With SHBG the model has no simple formula, so the page can't recompute it in the
4	browser. This script runs the Python model and replaces the data block between
5	the /*DATA*/ and /*END DATA*/ markers in the page.
6	
7	Usage:  python scripts/export_comparison_data.py
8	"""
9	
10	import json
11	import re
12	import sys
13	from pathlib import Path
14	
15	import numpy as np
16	
17	ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
18	sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT / "src"))
19	
20	from minipill.params import LEVONORGESTREL, LEVONORGESTREL_DOSE_MG, SHBG  # noqa: E402
21	from minipill.pk import mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml, simulate  # noqa: E402
22	
23	DAY = 24.0
24	PAGE = ROOT / "app" / "pill_comparison.html"
25	PACK = [d * DAY for d in range(21)]
26	DUE = 14 * DAY  # the day-15 pill
27	MONTH_STEP, LATE_STEP = 0.2, 0.25  # hours
28	LATE_WINDOW = (-24.0, 96.0)  # hours around DUE
29	LATE_OPTIONS = [x / 2 for x in range(48)] + ["skip", "skip2"]  # 0, 0.5, ... 23.5 h late
30	
31	
32	def run(doses, t):
33	    sim = simulate(LEVONORGESTREL, sorted(doses), LEVONORGESTREL_DOSE_MG, t, shbg=SHBG)
34	    return mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(sim.conc), sim.shbg
35	
36	
37	def scenario(late):
38	    if late == "skip":
39	        return [d for d in PACK if d != DUE]
40	    if late == "skip2":  # CDC: pills 15 and 16 missed; missed pill + pill 17 taken together at +48 h
41	        return [d for d in PACK if d not in (DUE, DUE + DAY)] + [DUE + 2 * DAY]
42	    return [d for d in PACK if d != DUE] + [DUE + late]
43	
44	
45	def main():
46	    t_month = np.arange(0, 28 * DAY + 1e-9, MONTH_STEP)
47	    c_month, s_month = run(PACK, t_month)
48	
49	    t_late = np.arange(0, DUE + LATE_WINDOW[1] + 1e-9, LATE_STEP)
50	    c_on, _ = run(PACK, t_late)
51	    low = c_on[int(round(DUE / LATE_STEP))]
52	    first = int(round((DUE + LATE_WINDOW[0]) / LATE_STEP))
53	    late = {}
54	    for opt in LATE_OPTIONS:
55	        c, _ = run(scenario(opt), t_late)
56	        late[opt if isinstance(opt, str) else f"{opt:g}"] = [round(100 * v / low, 1) for v in c[first:]]
57	
58	    data = {
59	        "monthStep": MONTH_STEP,
60	        "month": [round(float(v), 4) for v in c_month],
61	        "shbg": [round(float(v), 2) for v in s_month],
62	        "lateStep": LATE_STEP,
63	        "lateStart": LATE_WINDOW[0],
64	        "usualLow": round(float(low), 4),
65	        "late": late,
66	    }
67	    block = "/*DATA*/ const LNG_SHBG = " + json.dumps(data, separators=(",", ":")) + "; /*END DATA*/"
68	    html = PAGE.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
69	    new, n = re.subn(r"/\*DATA\*/.*?/\*END DATA\*/", lambda _: block, html, flags=re.S)
70	    if n != 1:
71	        raise SystemExit("data markers not found in page")
72	    PAGE.write_text(new, encoding="utf-8")
73	    print(f"Wrote {len(block) / 1024:.0f} KB of data; usual low {low:.3f} ng/mL")
74	
75	
76	if __name__ == "__main__":
77	    main()

#    and distribution apart, so ka and alpha individually are not well determined;

    V_L=18.7,  # L, central volume, fitted

import numpy as np
import pytest

from minipill.params import (
    ALESSE_DAY1, ALESSE_SHBG_NMOL_L, ALESSE_STEADY_STATE, ALESSE_TABLE_I, LEVONORGESTREL, LEVONORGESTREL_1C, SHBG,
    LEVONORGESTREL_DOSE_MG, NORETHINDRONE, NORETHINDRONE_1C, NORETHINDRONE_DOSE_MG, NORETHINDRONE_LABEL,
)
from minipill.pk import (
    Drug, SHBGEffect, accumulation_ratio, bateman, exact_single_dose, ka_from_tmax, mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml,
    mg_per_l_to_pg_per_ml, simulate, tmax,
)

DAY = 24.0
# Generic levonorgestrel-like drug (30 h half-life) for checks that don't need real values.
SLOW = Drug.one_compartment(name="slow", half_life_h=30.0, ka=ka_from_tmax(1.5, 30.0), F=1.0, V_L=100.0)
# Generic two-compartment drug with well-separated rates.
TWO_COMP = Drug(name="two-comp", ka=2.0, F=0.8, V_L=20.0, k10=0.3, k12=0.6, k21=0.1)

ONE_COMP_DRUGS = [NORETHINDRONE_1C, LEVONORGESTREL_1C, SLOW]
TWO_COMP_DRUGS = [NORETHINDRONE, LEVONORGESTREL, TWO_COMP]
ALL_DRUGS = ONE_COMP_DRUGS + TWO_COMP_DRUGS


def ids(d):
    return d.name


# --- The numerical solver ---------------------------------------------------

@pytest.mark.parametrize("drug", ONE_COMP_DRUGS, ids=ids)
# --- Levonorgestrel vs. Alesse (no SHBG effect yet) ------------------------------

def _levonorgestrel_single_dose(drug, hours=DAY):
    t = np.linspace(0, hours, int(hours * 1000) + 1)
    c = mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(simulate(drug, [0], LEVONORGESTREL_DOSE_MG, t).conc)
    return t, c


def test_levonorgestrel_matches_alesse_day1():
    t, c = _levonorgestrel_single_dose(LEVONORGESTREL)
    label = ALESSE_DAY1
    assert t[np.argmax(c)] == pytest.approx(label["tmax_h"], abs=0.05)
    assert c.max() == pytest.approx(label["cmax_ng_ml"], rel=0.02)
    auc = mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(LEVONORGESTREL.F * LEVONORGESTREL_DOSE_MG / LEVONORGESTREL.clearance_L_per_h)
    assert auc == pytest.approx(label["auc_ng_h_ml"], rel=0.02)
    assert LEVONORGESTREL.terminal_half_life_h == pytest.approx(label["half_life_h"], rel=0.02)


def test_levonorgestrel_one_compartment_underpredicts_peak():
    """Same failure as norethindrone: the label's CL/F and Vz/F give a peak ~4x too low."""
    t, c = _levonorgestrel_single_dose(LEVONORGESTREL_1C)
    assert t[np.argmax(c)] == pytest.approx(ALESSE_DAY1["tmax_h"], abs=0.01)
    assert c.max() == pytest.approx(0.69, abs=0.01)
    assert ALESSE_DAY1["cmax_ng_ml"] / c.max() == pytest.approx(4.0, abs=0.1)


def test_without_shbg_day21_auc_is_about_half_of_alesse():
    """Behavior the science requires: without SHBG, a linear model's day-21 AUC over one
    dosing interval equals the day-1 AUC (35.2), but Alesse measured 68.3 ng*h/mL.
    The missing factor (~1.9) is the SHBG effect, matching the CL/F fall 53.7 -> 28.4."""
    t = np.linspace(20 * DAY, 21 * DAY, 2401)
    sim = simulate(LEVONORGESTREL, np.arange(21) * DAY, LEVONORGESTREL_DOSE_MG, np.concatenate([[0.0], t]))
    c = mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(sim.conc[1:])
    auc_day21 = np.trapezoid(c, t)
    assert auc_day21 == pytest.approx(ALESSE_DAY1["auc_ng_h_ml"], rel=0.02)
    label_auc21, label_cl1, label_cl21 = ALESSE_TABLE_I[21][0], ALESSE_TABLE_I[1][1], ALESSE_TABLE_I[21][1]
    assert label_auc21 / auc_day21 == pytest.approx(label_cl1 / label_cl21, rel=0.05)
    # Trough before the next pill: ~0.84 ng/mL without SHBG vs. 1.9 ng/mL measured.
    assert c[-1] == pytest.approx(0.84, abs=0.02)
    assert c[-1] < 0.5 * ALESSE_STEADY_STATE["cmin_ng_ml"]

def test_shbg_predicts_steady_state_low_and_peak(pack_with_shbg):
    """Not fitted: the day-21 low and peak land within the label's mean ± SD."""
    _, peak, low = _day(pack_with_shbg, 21)

    LEVONORGESTREL_DOSE_MG, NORETHINDRONE, NORETHINDRONE_1C, NORETHINDRONE_DOSE_MG, NORETHINDRONE_LABEL,
)

<title>Minipill vs. Combined Pill</title>
<meta name="claude:viewport-fit-sides" content="cover">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Figtree:wght@400;500;600;700&family=JetBrains+Mono:wght@400;500&display=swap">
<style>
/* Layout: one reading column; every chart puts both pills on one axis (blue = minipill, orange = combined pill) */
:root {
  --bg: #f6f7f9;
  --surface: #ffffff;
  --ink: #14171c;
  --ink-2: #4a5160;
  --muted: #7a8190;
  --grid: #e4e7ec;
  --rule: #d5d9e0;
  --mini: #2a78d6;
  --combo: #eb6834;
  --focus: #2a78d6;
  --placebo: #eef0f3;
  --font-body: "Figtree", "Segoe UI", system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif;
  --font-data: "JetBrains Mono", ui-monospace, "Cascadia Mono", Consolas, monospace;
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:not([data-theme="light"]) {
    color-scheme: dark;
    --bg: #101216; --surface: #171a20; --ink: #eceef2; --ink-2: #b6bcc8; --muted: #858c9a;
    --grid: #262a32; --rule: #333844; --mini: #3987e5; --combo: #d95926; --focus: #6da7ec; --placebo: #1d2027;
  }
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] {
  color-scheme: dark;
  --bg: #101216; --surface: #171a20; --ink: #eceef2; --ink-2: #b6bcc8; --muted: #858c9a;
  --grid: #262a32; --rule: #333844; --mini: #3987e5; --combo: #d95926; --focus: #6da7ec; --placebo: #1d2027;
}

* { box-sizing: border-box; }
body {
  background: var(--bg); color: var(--ink); font-family: var(--font-body); font-size: 15px; line-height: 1.55;
  padding-left: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px));
  padding-right: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px));
  padding-block: 40px 56px;
}
main { max-width: 880px; margin: 0 auto; display: grid; gap: 40px; }
h1, h2 { text-wrap: balance; margin: 0; }
h1 { font-size: clamp(28px, 4.5vw, 38px); font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: -0.015em; line-height: 1.15; }
h2 { font-size: 21px; font-weight: 650; letter-spacing: -0.005em; }
p { margin: 0; max-width: 66ch; }
b, strong { font-weight: 650; }
.eyebrow { font-family: var(--font-data); font-size: 12px; letter-spacing: 0.06em; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--muted); }
header { display: grid; gap: 12px; }
.lede { color: var(--ink-2); font-size: 16.5px; }
section { display: grid; gap: 16px; }
.section-head { display: grid; gap: 6px; }
.section-head p { color: var(--ink-2); }
.say { font-size: 16px; color: var(--ink) !important; }
.say .tag { font-family: var(--font-data); font-size: 11px; letter-spacing: 0.06em; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--mini); margin-right: 8px; }

.plain { background: var(--surface); border: 1px solid var(--rule); border-radius: 10px; padding: 16px 18px; display: grid; gap: 10px; }
.plain h2 { font-size: 17px; }
.plain ul { margin: 0; padding-left: 1.1em; display: grid; gap: 8px; max-width: 70ch; }

.panel { background: var(--surface); border: 1px solid var(--rule); border-radius: 10px; padding: 16px 16px 12px; display: grid; gap: 12px; }
.toolbar { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 12px 20px; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; }
.legend { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 6px 18px; font-size: 13.5px; color: var(--ink-2); }
.legend span { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px; }
.legend svg { flex: none; }

.seg { display: inline-flex; flex-wrap: wrap; border: 1px solid var(--rule); border-radius: 7px; overflow: hidden; }
.seg button { font: 500 13px var(--font-body); color: var(--ink-2); background: transparent; border: 0; padding: 6px 12px; cursor: pointer; }
.seg button + button { border-left: 1px solid var(--rule); }
.seg button[aria-pressed="true"] { background: var(--ink); color: var(--surface); }
button:focus-visible, input:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--focus); outline-offset: 2px; }
.check { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px; font-size: 13.5px; color: var(--ink-2); cursor: pointer; }
.check input { accent-color: var(--ink); }

.chart { position: relative; width: 100%; }
.chart svg { display: block; width: 100%; height: auto; overflow: visible; }
.chart text { font-family: var(--font-data); font-size: 11px; fill: var(--muted); }
.chart .axis-title { font-family: var(--font-body); font-size: 12px; fill: var(--ink-2); }
.chart .gridline { stroke: var(--grid); stroke-width: 1; }
.chart .baseline-axis { stroke: var(--rule); stroke-width: 1; }
.chart .line { fill: none; stroke-width: 2; stroke-linejoin: round; stroke-linecap: round; }
.chart .mini { stroke: var(--mini); }
.chart .combo { stroke: var(--combo); }
.chart .dash { stroke-dasharray: 6 5; stroke-width: 1.5; }
.chart .faint { opacity: 0.4; stroke-width: 1.5; }
.chart .ref { stroke: var(--ink-2); stroke-width: 1.25; stroke-dasharray: 2 4; fill: none; }
.chart .ref-label { fill: var(--ink-2); font-family: var(--font-body); font-size: 12px; }
.chart .errbar { stroke: var(--ink); stroke-width: 1.5; fill: none; }
.chart .pt { stroke: var(--surface); stroke-width: 2; }
.chart .crosshair { stroke: var(--ink-2); stroke-width: 1; opacity: 0.6; }
.chart .hover-dot { stroke: var(--surface); stroke-width: 2; }
.chart .placebo { fill: var(--placebo); }
.chart .band-label { font-family: var(--font-body); font-size: 12px; fill: var(--muted); }
.chart .pill-due { fill: var(--ink-2); }

.tip { position: absolute; pointer-events: none; z-index: 2; background: var(--surface); color: var(--ink); border: 1px solid var(--rule); border-radius: 8px; box-shadow: 0 6px 20px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.12); padding: 8px 10px; font-size: 12.5px; min-width: 190px; dis
.tip .tip-head { font-family: var(--font-data); font-size: 11.5px; color: var(--muted); }
.tip .row { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px; justify-content: space-between; }
.tip .row span:first-child { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 6px; color: var(--ink-2); }
.tip .v { font-family: var(--font-data); font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
.sw { width: 12px; height: 3px; border-radius: 2px; display: inline-block; }

.table-wrap { overflow-x: auto; }
table { border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; font-size: 14px; min-width: 560px; }
th, td { text-align: right; padding: 8px 10px; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--grid); white-space: nowrap; }
th:first-child, td:first-child { text-align: left; }
thead th { font-weight: 600; color: var(--ink-2); font-size: 12.5px; border-bottom-color: var(--rule); }
td { font-family: var(--font-data); font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; font-size: 13px; }
td:first-child { font-family: var(--font-body); font-size: 14px; }
td.note { font-family: var(--font-body); font-size: 12.5px; color: var(--muted); white-space: normal; text-align: left; }
.dot { display: inline-block; width: 9px; height: 9px; border-radius: 50%; margin-right: 8px; vertical-align: 0; }
tbody tr:last-child td { border-bottom: 0; }

.controls { display: grid; gap: 10px; }
.slider-row { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; align-items: center; gap: 10px 16px; }
.slider-row label { font-weight: 600; font-size: 14px; }
.slider-row input[type="range"] { flex: 1 1 220px; accent-color: var(--ink); }
.late-val { font-family: var(--font-data); font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; font-size: 14px; min-width: 9ch; }

.versus { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 1px; background: var(--rule); border: 1px solid var(--rule); border-radius: 10px; overflow: hidden; }
.vcol { background: var(--surface); padding: 14px 16px; display: grid; gap: 10px; align-content: start; }
.vcol h3 { margin: 0; font-size: 15px; font-weight: 650; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px; }
.vrow { display: grid; gap: 1px; }
.vrow .k { font-size: 12.5px; color: var(--ink-2); }
.vrow .n { font-family: var(--font-data); font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; font-size: 21px; font-weight: 500; }
.vrow .n small { font-size: 13px; color: var(--muted); font-weight: 400; }
.summary { font-size: 15.5px; }
.explain { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)); gap: 12px; }
.step { background: var(--surface); border: 1px solid var(--rule); border-radius: 10px; padding: 14px 16px; display: grid; gap: 6px; align-content: start; }
.step h3 { margin: 0; font-size: 15px; font-weight: 650; }
.step p { font-size: 14.5px; color: var(--ink-2); }
.chain { font-family: var(--font-data); font-size: 13px; color: var(--ink); background: var(--surface); border: 1px solid var(--rule); border-radius: 10px; padding: 12px 16px; overflow-x: auto; white-space: nowrap; }
.chain b { color: var(--combo); font-weight: 500; }
.callout { border-left: 3px solid var(--combo); padding: 4px 0 4px 14px; color: var(--ink-2); }

footer { color: var(--muted); font-size: 13px; display: grid; gap: 6px; border-top: 1px solid var(--rule); padding-top: 16px; }
footer p { max-width: 80ch; }

1:# Why Is the Minipill So Strict?
15:## In plain terms
26:## The question
42:## What the program does
52:## How the model works
79:### SHBG and the combined pill
99:## How I know it's right
156:## Running it
183:## Repository layout
196:## Key parameters
207:## Assumptions and limitations
210:- Parameters are averages from label studies. Real people vary, and published data show that body weight can roughly double levonorgestrel's half-life.
215:## Possible extensions
217:- **Body weight:** reproduce published differences in levonorgestrel kinetics between normal-BMI and obese users (Edelman et al., 2009), then see what the model predicts for the minipill, where no such data exist.
220:## Sources
229:- Edelman, A. B., et al. (2009). [Impact of obesity on oral contraceptive pharmacokinetics and hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian activity](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2736633). *Contraception*, 80(2), 119–127.
231:## About

## Key parameters

Full tables, with sources for every value, are in [`sources/`](sources/).

| Hormone | Half-life | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Norethindrone (minipill) | 7.7 ± 0.5 h | Peak ≈ 1.2 h after a dose; taken daily with no break |
| Levonorgestrel (combined) | ≈ 30 h single dose (Seasonale); 34 h on day 1 and 36 ± 13 h at steady state (Alesse) | Binds SHBG; rises about 2-fold over the cycle with Alesse (Levette label says 3- to 4-fold) |
| SHBG (combined pill) | Half-way to its plateau in ≈ 3.2 days (fitted) | 57 → 93.5 nmol/L with daily estrogen; slows levonorgestrel clearance as (57 / SHBG)^1.33 |
| Ethinyl estradiol (combined) | ≈ 15 h single dose; 18 ± 4.7 h at steady state | Raises SHBG ≈ 1.7-fold; broken down partly by CYP3A4 |

## Assumptions and limitations

- Hormone level is used as a stand-in for protection. In reality, the minipill also works through cervical mucus, and the model doesn't simulate ovulation itself.
- Parameters are averages from label studies. Real people vary, and published data show that body weight can roughly double levonorgestrel's half-life.
- The SHBG effect is calibrated to one study (Alesse, 22 women), not measured directly. SHBG stands for the whole estrogen effect on levonorgestrel's clearance, and the shrinking volume of distribution isn't modeled, so week-3 peaks are underpredicted.
- Ethinyl estradiol itself isn't simulated: estrogen counts as "on" for 24 h after each active pill.
- Drug interactions, food, and vomiting or diarrhea are not modeled (yet).

## Possible extensions

- **Body weight:** reproduce published differences in levonorgestrel kinetics between normal-BMI and obese users (Edelman et al., 2009), then see what the model predicts for the minipill, where no such data exist.
- **Drug interactions:** a drug like rifampin speeds up the enzyme that breaks down ethinyl estradiol, which should lower SHBG and then levonorgestrel.

## Sources

- Teorell, T. (1937). Kinetics of distribution of substances administered to the body. *Archives Internationales de Pharmacodynamie et de Thérapie*, 57.

p='README.md'
s=open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
def rep(a,b):
    global s
    assert s.count(a)==1,a; s=s.replace(a,b)
rep("""## How I know it's right""","""### Body size (BMI)

**The data.** Edelman et al. (2009) gave Alesse to 10 women of normal BMI (mean 21.9) and 10 with obesity (mean 37.3). Levonorgestrel's half-life was 25.6 h vs. 52.1 h; volume of distribution and SHBG didn't differ. Same volume with twice the half-life means clearance × 0.49.

**In the model.** `clearance_factor_for_bmi` in `params.py` scales `k10` (clearance) by 1 up to BMI 21.9, by 0.49 from 37.3 up, and smoothly in between (log of clearance linear in BMI). Nothing else changes. The comparison page takes weight and height (kg/cm or lb/ft-in), works out BMI and redraws every chart.

**Assumptions.** Only two groups were measured, so the in-between curve is a guess; it stays flat above 37.3 because the heaviest women in the study (BMI ≥ 40) looked like the rest of the obese group. The label studies are taken to be normal-BMI women. **Norethindrone has no BMI data**: the minipill gets the same change as an untested assumption.

**Check.** Clearance matches by construction. Levonorgestrel's half-life rises ×1.75 in the model (34 → 60 h) vs. ×2.03 measured, because the two-compartment model can't change both with `k10` alone.

**Result.** Slower clearance keeps levels higher, so in the model a higher BMI makes a late pill dip *less*:

| BMI | Minipill, 3 h late | Combined, 3 h late | Minipill, 1 missed | Combined, 1 missed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 21.9 | 23% | 4% | 88% | 28% |
| 30 | 20% | 3% | 83% | 21% |
| 37.3 | 16% | 2% | 76% | 16% |

This doesn't capture Edelman's concern, which is about the start of each pack: obese women took about twice as long to reach steady levels, and had a lower first-day peak (1.9 vs. 2.5 ng/mL, not statistically significant). Slower clearance alone can't produce a lower peak, so whatever caused it isn't in the model.

## How I know it's right""")
rep("""- Parameters are averages from label studies. Real people vary, and published data show that body weight can roughly double levonorgestrel's half-life.""",
"""- Parameters are averages from label studies. Real people vary. Body size changes only clearance, from one small study of levonorgestrel (see "Body size"); the same change is assumed for norethindrone.""")
rep("""- **Body weight:** reproduce published differences in levonorgestrel kinetics between normal-BMI and obese users (Edelman et al., 2009), then see what the model predicts for the minipill, where no such data exist.
""","""- **Body size, start of pack:** model the first week after the placebo week, where Edelman et al. saw the obese group's risk, and look for what could lower the first-day peak (absorption, volume).
""")
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)

content.text:
The comparison page now asks for weight and height (kg/cm or lb/ft-in, plus a weight slider), works out BMI, and redraws every BMI-dependent chart. I tested it in headless Chrome. At the default 60 kg / 166 cm it gives exactly the old results, and at higher BMIs it matches the Python model. All 57 tests pass, 15 of them new.

**How weight works in the model.** Edelman 2009 found levonorgestrel's half-life was 25.6 h at normal BMI (21.9) and 52.1 h in obese women (37.3), with no difference in volume of distribution. Same volume with twice the half-life means the body clears it at 0.49× the normal rate. The model uses that, with your three choices:
- Weight and height go in; BMI is worked out from them.
- Clearance is normal up to BMI 21.9, falls smoothly to 0.49× at 37.3, and stays flat above that.
- The minipill gets the same change, labelled on the page as an untested assumption, because there's no data for norethindrone.

The model's levonorgestrel half-life rises 1.75× (34 → 60 h), short of the study's 2.03×. The model can't match both clearance and half-life by changing one rate, so I matched clearance.

**The result goes against the usual worry.** In the model, a higher BMI makes a late pill dip *less* for both pills, because slower clearance keeps levels higher:

| BMI | Minipill, 3 h late | Combined, 3 h late | Minipill, 1 missed | Combined, 1 missed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 21.9 | 23% | 4% | 88% | 28% |
| 37.3 | 16% | 2% | 76% | 16% |

Edelman's concern was something this model doesn't capture: obese women took twice as long to reach steady levels at the **start** of each pack, and had a lower first-day peak. Slower clearance alone can't produce a lower peak. The page and the README both say this rather than presenting the model's result as the whole story. Modelling the start of the pack is now listed as a possible extension.

**What changed:**
- [pk.py](src/minipill/pk.py): `Drug.with_clearance_scaled`, plus `single_dose_terms`, which `exact_single_dose` now uses.
- [params.py](src/minipill/params.py): the Edelman data and `clearance_factor_for_bmi`.
- [export_comparison_data.py](scripts/export_comparison_data.py): exports nine BMIs from 21.9 to 37.3, and the page blends between neighbouring ones. The export takes about 70 seconds.
- [pill_comparison.html](app/pill_comparison.html): new "Body size" section, and BMI tags on the charts that change. The page grew from 0.2 to 1.5 MB.
- [README.md](README.md): "Body size (BMI)" section.
